neutral_facts.value: The prosecution alleged that on 13.11.2011, at 9:30 p.m., the victim, Narayan Singh, was shot dead at his home in Village Binjana, District Dewas, Madhya Pradesh. The victim's mother, Rachna Bai, testified that she and the victim were sleeping when someone called out the victim's name, prompting him to open the door. A gunshot was heard, and shortly after, a second gunshot struck the victim in the chest, causing him to fall. Rachna Bai saw her daughter-in-law and the victim's son standing on the opposite side of the house and two individuals with their faces covered fleeing the scene on a motorcycle. The prosecution's primary evidence against the appellant was the recovery of a pistol from him and a ballistic report confirming that the bullet recovered from the victim's body was fired from the recovered pistol. There were no eyewitnesses to the crime, and the case against the appellant rested entirely on circumstantial evidence.

quotes.text: The prosecution's primary evidence against the appellant, Santosh @ Rajesh @ Gopal, also referenced in the impugned judgment, is the recovery (Exhibit P-6) of a pistol and the ballistic report (Exhibit P-57), which confirms that the bullet (Exhibit B-1) recovered from the body of the victim, Narayan Singh, was fired from the country-made pistol (Exhibit A-1 and C-1). There is evidence to show that the pistol was recovered (Exhibit P-6) from the appellant, Santosh @ Rajesh @ Gopal, and we would accept the said version of the prosecution.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the absence of corroborative evidence directly linking the appellant to the crime introduces a significant gap in the chain of circumstances, failing to establish a hypothesis of guilt that conclusively excludes all other reasonable possibilities.

quotes.text: The absence of any corroborative evidence directly linking the appellant to the crime introduces a significant gap in facts as alleged in the chain of circumstances.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that where the case rests entirely on circumstantial evidence, a finding of guilt is justified only if all incriminating facts and circumstances are incompatible with the accused's innocence, and there is a complete chain of evidence excluding all other possibilities.

quotes.text: Where the case rests entirely on circumstantial evidence, a finding of guilt is justified only if all the incriminating facts and circumstances are incompatible with the accused’s innocence.
